title: The ambrosial hour
hook: Sikhs rise before dawn for prayer and meditation

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was guru: a teacher whose words carry weight, and the two tests, do they know it, do they live it. Your line was choose with care.

An alarm goes off with nothing scheduled after it. No meeting, no shift, no school bell. Someone gets up anyway, washes, wraps a turban or covers their hair, and sits down on the floor with a small book, or walks to the gurdwara, where the doors are already open. Outside, the birds haven't started. The day hasn't asked for anything yet. That's the point. Today the path turns from Hindu ways to Sikh ways, and it starts before the sun.
screen: `AN ALARM, NOTHING SCHEDULED.` → `THE DOORS ARE ALREADY OPEN.` → `THE DAY HASN'T ASKED YET.`

segments.voice: Amrit vela: the ambrosial hour, the early hours before dawn. Amrit is nectar, the drink of immortality, and it's also the word Sikhs use for the sweetened water of initiation. Vela is the time, the hour. Put together: the nectar time. It comes right at the start of the Guru Granth Sahib, in Guru Nanak's Japji. The fourth stanza says, in paraphrase: in the ambrosial hours, meditate on the true Name, and reflect on God's greatness. Two jobs for the early hour: remember the Name, and consider how great is the one it names. A later Guru, Guru Ram Das, is even more practical. In a passage of the Guru Granth Sahib he describes someone who calls themselves a Sikh of the true Guru. That person, he says, rises early and meditates on the Name, makes the effort in the early morning, bathes in the pool of nectar, and then goes on through the day singing the Guru's word. Notice the order. In the passage, the early hour isn't an escape from the day. It's the start of it, and the day is meant to carry what was found there. And why so early? The texts don't give a lecture on it. But the hour has its own texture. The phone hasn't buzzed. Nobody needs you. The mind hasn't filled up yet. Whatever you put in first, it seems, has room.
screen: `AMRIT VELA: THE NECTAR TIME.` · `JAPJI: THE NAME, AND GOD'S GREATNESS.` · `RISE EARLY, BATHE, REMEMBER.` · `THE START OF THE DAY, NOT AN ESCAPE.` · then, large: `WHAT GOES IN FIRST HAS ROOM.`

segments.voice: Sit as if it were that hour: dim a light if you can, settle, and notice what the room sounds like when it isn't asking for anything. If you pray, you can remember a name of God you hold dear; if you don't, just sit in the quiet.
Amrit vela. The ambrosial hour before dawn, when Sikhs who keep it rise to remember the Name before the day begins asking. Today's word.
Your line: the early hour. Before the phone, before the day's first ask, the doors are already open. Day one thousand three hundred ninety-nine.

howItsDone: Sikhs who keep the amrit vela rise in the hours before dawn, bathe, and give the time to meditation on the Name and the morning prayers, at home or in the gurdwara, before the work of the day.
